title: 8th Generation Rogan Art Master Craftsperson

awards.name: National Award
awards.authority: Ministry of Textiles, Govt. of India

verifiedBy: Development Commissioner (Handicrafts), Ministry of Textiles
bio: Padma Shri Abdul Gafur Khatri is the patriarch of the sole surviving family in India preserving the 400-year-old Persian-origin Rogan art. When the craft faced near-total extinction with only six surviving practitioners, Abdul Gafur broke centuries-old male-only tradition to train more than 300 village women, ensuring community survival. In 2014, Prime Minister Narendra Modi famously presented two of his signature Tree of Life Rogan paintings to US President Barack Obama.
techniques: Boiled castor oil heated continuously for 12 hours until it forms a thick jelly residue called 'Rogan'. This base is emulsified with natural earth minerals and stone pigments. Using a 6-inch blunt brass stylus ('Kalam') held in the right hand, the artisan draws thread-like paint loops onto stretched silk or khadi cotton balanced on the left palm—without any preparatory sketches. The fabric is then folded in half to create mirror-image symmetry.

bio: Shah Rasheed Ahmed Quadri is internationally celebrated for reviving the 600-year-old metal art of Bidar, introduced under the Bahmani Sultanate in the 14th century. Master Quadri revolutionized the craft by introducing geometric sheet inlays, intricate floral meenakari in pure silver, and modern functional silhouettes like pen stands, boxes, and contemporary tableware, while preserving the sacred soil-blackening ritual.
techniques: The metal body is cast from an alloy of copper and zinc in a 1:16 ratio. The rough casting is smoothed with files, temporarily darkened with copper sulphate, and patterns are chiseled freehand with pointed steel chisels. Pure 99.9% fine silver wire or cut sheet is meticulously hammered into the grooves ('Tarkashi' wire inlay and 'Tehnishan' sheet inlay). Finally, the piece is boiled in a unique chemical paste composed of ammonium chloride and rare unoxidized soil excavated from the foundations of Bidar Fort, which turns the zinc pitch black while leaving silver brilliant white.

He is renowned for perfecting turquoise, cobalt, and emerald glazes on non-clay dough, crafting massive decorative urns and intricate architectural wall tiles that decorate heritage palaces across Rajasthan and global consulates.
techniques: Unlike traditional ceramics, Jaipur Blue Pottery uses no clay. Objects are formed in open plaster moulds, air-dried, coated with quartz-powder slip, painted with oxide colors (cobalt oxide for deep blue, copper oxide for turquoise, iron oxide for brown) using fine squirrel hair brushes, glazed with glass-borax solution, and single-fired in wood or gas kilns at 800°C–850°C.

bio: Ghulam Hassan Mir is a revered fifth-generation master weaver from Kanihama—the historical village whose very name derives from 'Kani' (meaning small wooden spool in Kashmiri). He weaves museum-grade Pashmina shawls using the needle-weave technique mentioned in the 16th-century Mughal chronicle Ain-i-Akbari. A single Jamawar Kani shawl woven in his workshop takes between 9 to 18 months of intensive, uninterrupted hand labor.
techniques: Woven on traditional four-pedal pit looms using 100% fine hand-spun Changthangi Pashmina cashmere (12–14 microns). The weaver decodes a rhythmic sung code called 'Talim' read out by the master artisan, recording the precise warp count for every single color change.

techniques: Canvas ('Patta') is prepared by bonding layers of cotton fabric using tamarind seed paste ('Niryas') and soft stone powder, dried and burnished with sea shells until it turns ivory-smooth. The incised grooves are rubbed with black lamp soot mixed with bean leaf extract, and excess is washed off to reveal sharp black lines.

bio: For over 700 years, the potters of Molela on the banks of River Banas have hand-modeled sacred hollow votive plaques for tribal priests ('Bhopas') belonging to the Bhil, Garasia, and Gujjar communities. Dinesh Chandra Kumhar is the revered Shilp Guru of this lineage, whose relief sculptures of Lord Devnarayan riding his blue horse and the multi-armed Goddess Chamunda grace temples and tribal shrines across Western India.
techniques: Clay is harvested strictly from the local Talaab (pond) silt and blended with donkey manure in a 3:1 ratio, providing natural fiber porosity that prevents cracking during firing. The plaque base is flattened on a cloth mat, and high-relief icons are hand-sculpted completely freehand using a small flat wooden spatula knife called 'Baldi'. The sculpted plaques dry in the shade for two weeks before being fired in primitive wood-fueled trench kilns. Finally painted with natural stone pigments and coated with acacia gum resin.

name: Bikash Biswas & Kalpana Karmakar
title: Preservers of 4,000-Year-Old Lost-Wax Dokra Metal Casting
verifiedBy: West Bengal Handicrafts Development Corp (Manjusha)
bio: Residing in Bikna Shilpagram, Bikash and Kalpana practice the oldest non-ferrous lost-wax metal casting method known to humanity—the exact technique used 4,500 years ago to cast the Indus Valley civilization's Dancing Girl of Mohenjo-daro. Their hollow brass castings are distinct for their primitive wire-wrapped texture, elongated limbs, and celebration of tribal folklore.
techniques: A clay core roughly resembling the final figure is fashioned from local ant-hill soil and paddy husk. Beeswax, resin from the Dammar Sal tree, and mustard oil are mixed, heated, and pushed through a wooden press with tiny perforations to create spaghetti-like wax threads. These threads are wound meticulously over the clay core to form clothing, jewelry, and features. Two additional layers of clay are applied, leaving pouring channels. The mold is heated in a pit furnace; the wax drains away, and molten recycled brass or bronze is poured into the vacuum. Once cooled, the outer clay shell is hammered open, revealing a one-of-a-kind sculpture that can never be duplicated.

bio: Rebuilding their entire village as 'Ajrakhpur' after the devastating 2001 Bhuj earthquake, Dr. Ismail Khatri's family has practiced the 16-step natural dyeing tradition of Ajrakh for nine generations. Revered by textile historians across the world, their geometric double-sided block prints reflect cosmic geometry using strictly plant and mineral dyes like indigo, madder root, harda, and iron scrap acetate.
techniques: The fabric undergoes a rigorous 16-stage process taking up to 3 weeks: 'Saaj' (washing in camel dung and soda), 'Kasanu' (tanning with Harda myrobalan powder), 'Rekh' (fine outline block printing with lime and acacia gum), and 'Katt' (black printing with fermented scrap iron and jaggery syrup). Multiple dips in natural fermented indigo vats and boiling in copper vats with dried Dhauro flowers and madder root yield intense crimson reds and celestial blues that resist fading over centuries.

name: N. Sivaraman Sthapathi
title: Chola Panchaloha Bronze Casting Shilp Guru
verifiedBy: Tamil Nadu Handicrafts Development Corp & Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) Approved
bio: Belonging to the direct architectural and sculpting lineage that cast the monumental bronzes of the Brihadisvara Temple under Raja Raja Chola I in 1010 CE, N. Sivaraman Sthapathi preserves the sacred art of 'Panchaloha' (five-metal alloy) casting. Adhering to the Sanskrit verses of the Shilpa Shastra, his iconic Nataraja, Ardhanarishvara, and Parvati statues grace world museums and temple sanctums.
techniques: The wax model ('Mezhugu') is sculpted from pure beeswax, dammar resin (Kungilium), and groundnut oil. Measurements follow the 'Talamana' canon based on multiples of the idol's own finger-breadth. The wax model is layered three times with fine alluvial silt harvested from the bed of River Kaveri, forming the 'Karu' mold. Reinforced with iron wires and baked in an open kiln, the melted wax drains out. The five-metal alloy ('Panchaloha'—predominantly copper, brass, lead, with ceremonial pinches of gold and silver) is liquefied in graphite crucibles at 1,100°C and poured in a continuous stream. Once cooled and unchiseled, details are carved using hand-tempered cold chisels.

bio: Bhoodan Pochampally was India's first craft product to receive Geographical Indication (GI) tag protection in 2004. C. techniques: Yarns of pure mulberry silk or fine cotton are wound onto specialized triangular peg frames ('Asu') to calculate design grids. Bundles of threads are tied with waterproof rubber ties according to mathematical graphs and dipped into dye baths. The process is repeated for every color in the palette. Once dry, the dyed warp is mounted on pit looms, and the weft is wound onto pirns. As the weaver throws the fly shuttle, warp and weft intersect to materialize complex diamond, parrot, and geometric motifs.

She paints directly onto handmade paper treated with cow-dung wash, rendering everyday rural life—women harvesting makhana (foxnuts) in waist-deep ponds, fishermen throwing nets, and village festivals.

name: Hemant Kumar & Bastar Tribal Guild
title: Masters of Bastar Wrought Iron Craft (Loha Shilp)

awards.name: National Handicrafts Award
awards.authority: Ministry of Textiles, Govt. of India

verifiedBy: Chhattisgarh Hastshilp Vikas Board (Shabari Emporium)
bio: The blacksmiths (Lohars) of the Gond and Maria tribes of Bastar have forged iron for millennia, originally crafting hunting arrowheads and farming sickles. Hemant Kumar leads a renowned artisanal cooperative that transformed this utilitarian metallurgy into expressive contemporary art—hand-forging scrap iron into slender antelopes, ceremonial oil lamps, and tall musicians without modern welding.
techniques: Crafted exclusively from recycled iron scrap, wrought rods, and discarded iron plates. Pieces of iron are heated red-hot in traditional open charcoal hearths fueled by manual goat-skin or hand bellows. While glowing red, the iron is beaten forcefully on an anvil using heavy hammers and cold-cut with chisels. No electrical welding or soldering is used; separate limbs and appendages are joined by hot-riveting or wrapping malleable heated iron collars around joints. Finally polished with mustard oil to produce a rust-resistant matte graphite finish.

name: Zakir Hussain Mir
title: Downtown Srinagar Wild Walnut Woodcarver

awards.name: National Merit Certificate
awards.authority: Ministry of Textiles, Govt. of India

verifiedBy: Craft Development Institute (CDI) Srinagar & J&K Handicrafts
bio: Carving in the winding historic alleys of Srinagar's Safa Kadal along the Jhelum River, Zakir Hussain Mir works with wild walnut timber (Juglans regia) harvested exclusively from fallen or dead trees in the Kashmir Valley. His family specializes in 'Jali' (open lattice fretwork) and 'Vaskar' (deep three-dimensional undercut relief) depicting wild chinar leaves, lotus blooms, and singing bulbuls.
techniques: Wild walnut logs are seasoned naturally in shaded courtyards for 2 to 3 years to ensure the wood does not warp or split in dry climates. Master Zakir employs four distinct carving depths: 'Undercut' (multi-layered 3D relief where flower stems are completely detached from background), 'Relief' (raised surface), 'Engraved' (fine shallow lines), and 'Open Lattice' (Jaali). Finished entirely by burnishing with smooth sea stones and walnut oil—no synthetic varnishes or stains are applied, allowing the natural dark heartwood grain to darken gracefully over decades.

name: Prabhu Dayal
title: Saharanpur Sheesham Brass Inlay Woodcraft Master
craftSubtype: Saharanpur Wood Carving & Brass Wire Inlay (Tarkashi)
verifiedBy: Export Promotion Council for Handicrafts & UP Handicrafts Board
bio: Known as the 'Wood City of India', Saharanpur produces world-class hand-carved furniture and decorative woodwork. Prabhu Dayal is a master artisan famed for resurrecting the difficult technique of 'Tarkashi'—embedding flattened brass wire into seasoned Sheesham (Indian Rosewood) to form intricate floral arabesques and geometric jaali screens.
techniques: Hardwood Sheesham timber is seasoned in solar kilns. Detailed floral patterns are drafted onto the wood with paper stencils. Using razor-sharp fine gouges, narrow trenches half-millimeter deep are cut along the lines. Thin flattened brass ribbon wire is embedded into these trenches and hammered level using a small mallet. The surface is then planed smooth and rubbed with sandpaper and beeswax, ensuring the brass glints seamlessly against dark brown rosewood.

name: Lakshmi Ammal
title: Elder & Master of Nilgiris Toda Tribal Embroidery (Pukhoor)

awards.name: National Tribal Welfare Craft Honor
awards.authority: Ministry of Tribal Affairs, Govt. of India

verifiedBy: Tribal Cooperative Marketing Development Federation of India (TRIFED)
bio: Lakshmi Ammal is an elder of the pastoral Toda tribe dwelling in the high-altitude grasslands of the Nilgiris Biosphere. For generations, Toda women have embroidered their sacred ceremonial mantle known as 'Poothkuli'—a heavy white woven shawl draped during weddings and funeral rites. The embroidery is executed without graph paper or markings, directly reflecting the horns of sacred buffaloes, wild mountain butterflies, and spiderwebs.
techniques: Embroidered on coarse, loosely woven unbleached white cotton cloth with red and black wool or cotton threads. The technique relies on counting the threads of the warp and weft. Because the threads are counted with surgical precision, the reverse side of the shawl is almost as neat and geometrically symmetrical as the front face, giving the illusion of an embossed weave rather than surface embroidery.

name: Sarat Chandra Mohapatra
title: Pipli Master of Royal Jagannath Applique Craft

awards.name: National Merit Award
awards.authority: Ministry of Textiles, Govt. of India

verifiedBy: Odisha State Co-operative Handicrafts Corporation (Utkalika)
bio: For centuries, the tailors ('Darjis') of Pipli village on the pilgrim highway to Puri have prepared the massive royal canopies, umbrellas (Chhati), and banners (Trasa) for Lord Jagannath's annual Ratha Yatra festival. Sarat Chandra Mohapatra carries forward this vibrant heritage, stitching cut-out silhouettes of peacocks, elephants, parrots, and lotus medallions onto contrasting fabric backdrops adorned with glass mirrors.
techniques: Shapes of flowers, birds, and deities are hand-cut from colored cotton fabrics. These motifs are basted onto a heavy contrasting base cloth. Edges are folded under and stitched using fine chain-stitch, buttonhole stitch, or satin stitch with contrasting cotton threads. Circular glass mirrors ('Tarpa') and decorative cord piping are hand-stitched into the center of flower blossoms and eyes of animals to catch the light.

name: Narmada Bai & Ramesh Bunkar
title: Holkar Heritage Maheshwari Handloom Weavers

awards.name: Madhya Pradesh State Weaving Award
awards.authority: MP Hastshilp Evam Hathkargha Vikas Nigam

verifiedBy: Madhya Pradesh Handloom Board & Rehwa Society Partner
bio: Woven on the serene stone ghats of the Narmada River, Maheshwari handloom was championed in the late 18th century by the legendary philosopher-queen Ahilyabai Holkar. Narmada Bai and Ramesh Bunkar belong to the traditional bunkar community weaving lightweight, lustrous silk-cotton sarees. Their distinguishing hallmark is the reversible border ('Bugdi'), allowing sarees to be draped on either side without losing aesthetic beauty.
techniques: Woven on traditional pit and frame looms using fine mulberry silk warp (which provides gossamer luster) and delicate Egyptian or cotton weft (which provides softness and breathability in Indian summers). The border patterns—such as 'Chatai' (matting), 'Kangira' (fortress ramparts), and 'Chameli Phool' (jasmine blossom)—are derived directly from the carved stone relief panels of the Maheshwar Fort. Woven with double-sided reversible borders that require meticulous shuttle tracking.
